items.text: WTI is at $84.77/bbl and Brent at $93.26/bbl, which sits higher than 74% of readings over the past five years, and the trend across recent observations is roughly flat. Energy is the single largest swing factor behind headline inflation volatility, which means it feeds directly into the Fed's reaction function and therefore into your base-rate assumptions. On the portfolio side, sustained moves here reset input costs for transport-, logistics-, chemicals- and manufacturing-exposed borrowers, and are worth stress-testing in any credit model that assumed energy costs stay near recent levels.

Payrolls added -23K in the latest report, against a +20K average across the last three readings, and unemployment stands at 4.1%. Weekly initial claims are running near 209K, with average hourly earnings up 3.1% year over year. Hiring momentum is the most reliable leading read on demand durability for growth-oriented credits: payroll deceleration typically shows up in borrower topline growth and covenant headroom a quarter or two before it appears in the credit metrics themselves. Wage growth running above pre-pandemic norms also keeps services inflation sticky, which matters for labor-intensive issuers where payroll is the dominant variable cost.

Headline CPI is running 3.3% year over year (-0.2pt versus the prior reading), with core CPI at 2.5% and core PCE — the metric the FOMC actually targets — at 3.3%. Producer prices are up 4.7% year over year, the earliest read on what is coming at borrower input costs. The central tension is the gap between volatile headline prints, which are largely energy-driven and mean-revert, and the stickier core measures that determine the policy path. For underwriting, the practical implication is to price to sticky rather than falling financing costs until core decelerates convincingly, and to watch pricing power closely at issuers absorbing input-cost inflation they cannot pass through.

The Fed funds target stands at 3.50–3.75%, the 10-year Treasury at 4.70% and the 2-year at 4.22%. The 10Y-minus-2Y curve sits at +48bp, holding its normal upward slope, which is generally constructive for credit: it is not pricing imminent recession and it widens the margin banks and direct lenders earn borrowing short and lending long. The front end is your fastest read on repricing of hike-versus-cut odds around each CPI, PCE and jobs print, while the long end drives enterprise valuations and refinancing math. Every floating-rate structure in the book keys off the short end, so a persistent move here changes the cost-of-capital assumption underneath new originations mid-process.

High-yield OAS is 271bp, tighter than 91% of the past five years, and roughly flat across recent observations. Investment-grade OAS is 79bp. Index spreads are the cleanest market-priced gauge of how much you are actually being paid for credit risk. The pattern worth watching for special situations sourcing is compression at the index level masking widening dispersion underneath: idiosyncratic stress tends to surface in specific issuers — leveraged, tariff-exposed, or facing near-term maturities — well before the benchmark moves. That dispersion, not the index level, is where the opportunity set originates.

Real GDP grew 1.5% (QoQ SAAR) in the most recent quarter and the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow is tracking +5.8% for the current quarter, an early read ahead of the official advance estimate. Below-trend but positive growth is the backdrop that supports growth-oriented positioning over distressed or turnaround exposure. A material downside surprise would shift the opportunity set the other way, toward stressed and special situations, so the gap between the nowcast and the official print is worth tracking as an early warning rather than waiting on the lagging release.

University of Michigan consumer sentiment is 49.5, lower than 98% of readings over the past five years, and the personal saving rate is 2.7%. Housing starts are running 1.43M SAAR against a 6.67% 30-year mortgage rate. Housing and the consumer are the most rate-sensitive parts of the demand picture and typically the first to register policy tightening. A low saving rate means spending is running ahead of income growth, which is durable while labor income holds but drains quickly if payroll growth decelerates — worth tracking alongside the jobs data for consumer-facing and housing-cycle-exposed borrowers.

themeCards.title: US Labor Market Divergence & Layoff Risk
themeCards.statusLine: Nonfarm payrolls collapsed to -23K in July while ISM Mfg employment surged—services sector hiring stalled sharply (ISM Svc employment 47.4). Suggests rotation out of services into goods but also latent weakness in the largest employment pillar.
themeCards.relevance: For special situations, this foreshadows potential distress in service-oriented businesses (hospitality, healthcare support, financial services back-office) that depend on hiring momentum. IG financials and discretionary credit face pressure if unemployment ticks higher; watch for covenant stress in leveraged service providers.

themeCards.title: Middle East Energy Corridor Disruption
themeCards.statusLine: Brent crude jumped 3.9% to $88.90 on Red Sea shipping constraints and geopolitical tensions. Port congestion and rerouting extending delivery times (supply index in ISM Mfg at 58.9, highest in months). Threat to sustained production if incidents escalate.
themeCards.relevance: Oil shocks historically spike IG spreads (airlines, shipping, retailers) and CCC credit. Dislocations in energy-intensive issuers and transport-heavy supply chains (automotive, logistics, chemicals) merit tactical screening. Credit hedges on energy-heavy CCC baskets warranted if Brent stays >$85.

themeCards.title: China Manufacturing in Contraction
themeCards.statusLine: Official NBS PMI fell to 49.2 in July (below 50 threshold) from 50.3, signaling factory contraction and weak external demand. Export orders under pressure despite AI tailwinds. Reflects sluggish domestic demand post-stimulus plateau.
themeCards.relevance: For credit, elevated China risk flows through US supply chains (semis, industrials, consumer goods). Corporates with China revenue/sourcing concentration face margin risk if Chinese demand stalls. Exporters to China (ag equipment, luxury, industrial goods) face lower pricing power. Monitor China credit stress as early indicator of EM spillover.

themeCards.title: Persistent Refinance Wall & Spread Compression
themeCards.statusLine: IG spreads at 78 bps and HY at 270 bps leave little cushion for credit events. Refinance cliff remains 2026–2028, with many issuers unable to refinance at higher rates. Mortgage rates sticky at 6.69% add household stress, reducing discretionary spending on services/retail.
themeCards.relevance: Special situations investors should hunt for single-name dislocations in names with near-term maturities or refinance risk (CRE CMBS, select IG corporates, leveraged buyouts with debt ladders). Spreads compress into illiquidity events; tactical entry points in beaten-down names may emerge if micro credit events ripple.

themeCards.title: Service-Sector Employment Cliff
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Services employment index plummeted to 47.4 in July from 51.2 in June—largest monthly drop in months—despite robust business activity (59.1). Hiring has collapsed while demand remains resilient, signaling potential wage moderation or layoff prep.
themeCards.relevance: If service-sector firms are cutting labor despite strong order flow, margin compression and covenant stress may follow. Healthcare, business services, and financial services names with high wage expense bases are vulnerable. Monitor 3Q earnings for margin guidance; early warning sign of a consumer squeeze or margin-fixing cycle.

themeCards.title: Inverted Curve Easing & Disinflation Narrative
themeCards.statusLine: 2s10s curve steepened to 47 bps (+4 bps); 10y yield fell 5 bps to 4.65% despite oil strength, signaling market repricing toward softer growth and slower Fed cuts. Core PCE (2.57%) and headline (3.46%) both decelerating cleanly. Inversion risk fading.
themeCards.relevance: Normalization of the curve de-risks certain IG credits (regional banks, duration-sensitive financials) but also signals slower economic momentum ahead. Special situations players should look for dislocation between long-duration and short-duration spreads; implied Fed cuts may be priced in, creating opportunity in near-term refinances at lower yields.

regime.label: Late-cycle / softening
regime.detail: credit spreads near cycle tights; labor market cooling; core inflation sticky at 3.3%; curve positively sloped.
